Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:14: And so, in the chapter "The Acquisition of Torah" (Avot, chapter 6), in the mishnah of Rabbi Meir, "whoever occupies himself with Torah for its own sake merits many things," and so on, it says at the end of its words, "and be modest, and slow to anger, and forgiving of his own insult" - for these things are a preparation for the acquisition of wisdom. "Modest," as it is written (Proverbs 11:2), "and with the modest is wisdom." "Slow to anger and forgiving of his own insult," for if he becomes angry his Torah is forgotten, as explained - we say in Tractate Sotah (21b): Rabbi Yochanan said, words of Torah endure only in one who makes himself as though he were nothing, as it is said (Job 28:12), "and wisdom, from where shall it be found?" - to this point his words. And one of the things through which Torah is acquired is being slow to anger with a good heart, and it appears to me that King Solomon, peace be upon him, said of this (Proverbs 14:29), "he who is slow to anger has great understanding, but he who is quick-tempered exalts folly."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:15: And Rabbi Yitzchak of Acre, peace be upon him, wrote that he heard from the mouth of Rabbi Meir, the student of Rabbi Yosef Gikatilla, peace be upon him, that his teacher, Rabbi Yosef Gikatilla, peace be upon him, said to him, that the man whose heart moves him to repair his attributes and straighten his ways and his deeds, and to pursue humility to the utmost degree of perfection, to be insulted and not insult, to hear his own disgrace and not respond - immediately the Shechinah shall rest upon him, and he shall not need to learn from flesh and blood, for the spirit of God shall teach him - to this point, relevant here.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:16: Further, the same author wrote elsewhere - these are its words: we found it written in the books of the Kabbalists who merited the true path, that one of the great repairs among the repairs for one who seeks knowledge of the LORD is that he be among the insulted, even by his own wife and household, whom he should not fear or be ashamed of, while he himself shall not be an insulter - all the more so with people who are not of his household, that he be insulted and not insult. And if he must reprimand [lit. insult] his household to turn them from the path of death, in which they transgress the will of the Omnipresent, and to straighten and guide them in the path of life, which is the path in which they do the will of the Omnipresent, let him reprimand in a manner that he not become angry in his heart, but let his heart always be joyful, cleaving to everything - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:17: And so it is written in Tanna DeVei Eliyahu (Zuta, chapter 4), copied in the Yalkut, Parashat Ki Tisa (remez 391) - these are its words: the Sages taught, be humble toward every person, and toward the people of your household more than toward every person. Further, in Tanna DeVei Eliyahu, Parashat Atem Nitzavim, on the verse "it is not too wondrous for you" (Deuteronomy 30:11) - these are its words: a person should always be humble in Torah and in fear of Heaven with his father, his mother, his wife, his children, the people of his household, his neighbors, his relatives, and those distant from him, and even with a Gentile in the marketplace - so that he be beloved above and cherished below, and accepted by creatures, and fill his days and years with a good name; and through this his wife and household shall fear him, as it is said (Deuteronomy 28:10), "and all the peoples of the earth shall see that the Name of the LORD is called upon you, and they shall fear you" - to this point, relevant here. And without doubt, whoever trains himself to be insulted by the people of his household and not to insult shall be humble toward all and acquire in his heart the attribute of humility - for if in his own house, where they are subjugated under his hand, he is insulted and does not insult, all the more so with others.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:18: And further, among the category of the merit of humility is what is said in Kiddushin (71a), that the [Explicit] Name is transmitted only to whoever is in the middle of his years and is not angry. And I heard a story from the pious Rabbi Yaakov Ashkenazi, of blessed memory, that he was a wondrous sage in wisdom, and wished to teach his wisdom to Rabbi Yehoshua the Pious, but first tested him regarding anger - for it was a tradition in their hands not to transmit the wisdom except to one who, when tested with anger, would not become angry - and he tested him six times, and he endured, but on the seventh he did not stand firm, and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:19: The tenth merit, which is the cause of all the merits mentioned, is that the Shechinah rests with the humble and the lowly, as explained in Sotah (5a), which we copied above (chapter 1), and the Shechinah flees from the proud and the angry, as explained above (chapter 2).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:20: And so it is further explained in the Mechilta (Parashat Yitro) - these are its words: "and Moses drew near to the thick darkness" (Exodus 20:18) - what caused him this? His humility, as it is said (Numbers 12:3), "and the man Moses was very humble" - its ultimate purpose is to cause the Shechinah to rest with man on earth, as it is said (Isaiah 57:15), "thus says the High and Exalted One who inhabits eternity, and holy is His Name; high and holy I dwell, and with the contrite and humble of spirit," and it says (ibid. 61:1), "the spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me to bring good tidings to the humble; He has sent me to bind up the brokenhearted," and it says (ibid. 66:2), "for all these My hand has made... and to this one I look, to the poor and contrite of spirit" - "the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit" (Psalms 51:19).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:21: And whoever is proud of heart causes the land to be defiled and the Shechinah to depart, as it is said (Psalms 101:5), "haughty of eyes and proud of heart, him I cannot [endure]" - and every proud heart is called an abomination, as it is said (Proverbs 16:5), "every proud heart is an abomination to the LORD" - and idolatry is called an abomination, as it is said (Deuteronomy 7:26), "and you shall not bring an abomination into your house" - just as idolatry defiles the land and causes the Shechinah to depart, so whoever is proud of heart defiles the land and causes the Shechinah to depart - to this point. And I heard, in the name of the Midrash, a proof that the proud are hated before Him, blessed be He, in that He commanded (Leviticus 2:11), "for no leaven and no honey shall you burn as an offering" - and the reason is that honey boils in fire and produces foam, and likewise leaven boils and rises, and this is an allusion to the proud - therefore no fire-offering to the LORD shall be made from it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:22: It follows that pride and anger resemble each other in this punishment - for just as the angry person defiles himself, being like idolatry, as explained, so he too causes the Shechinah to depart, like the angry person.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:23: And after a person contemplates all the merits belonging to one who is humble, lowly, and does not insist on his own rights, as we have explained, he shall see with his intellect's eye that it is far more fitting for him to bear a small suffering for a great reward, than to lose all the merits mentioned in a single moment, and come to cause great loss - that his soul and the Shechinah depart from him - and until he returns, how much toil is needed until the spirit of impurity departs from within him, as explained in the Zohar, which said, "would that he be sanctified," and said, "and once it has fled from him once, how much must a person do until it returns to its place" - and thus a sinner shall lose great goodness.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:24: And this is a parable of a person who has in his hand a pitcher of water and a skin of balsam oil, and some trouble befalls him, and he must necessarily release from his hand one of them, which shall be lost - is it not certainly the way of reason that he sacrifice the small loss, which is the pitcher of water, in order to gain the great profit, which is the balsam in his hand? And if he does the opposite, he is certainly a fool. In exactly this manner is the matter of anger: for if a person endures not responding to his own disgrace, and forgoes the honor of his body, which is a small loss - not a loss at all, from the eye of reason - he shall gain a great profit for the level of his soul, that his transgressions shall be forgiven him, as we have elaborated in the other merits mentioned.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:25: Further, another way so that he not come to anger is that he think that the sufferings through which sins are atoned are two different aspects: either accepting suffering upon himself through fasts, sackcloth, and ashes, as King David, peace be upon him, did, or through the death of children, which is an atoning altar, as is known - and likewise death itself atones for everything, even the profanation of the Name, when repentance preceded it, as explained in the divisions of atonement that Rabbi Yishmael used to expound (Yoma 86a). Now, all these are difficult for a person to bear, and are very bitter, especially the death of children or one's own death - and behold, a person mortifies himself with mortifications for the atonement of his sins, and sometimes these involve neglect of Torah and neglect of prayer - how pleasant it would be for him to accept light sufferings that involve no neglect of Torah and prayer, and to accept them with love for the atonement of his sins, and to rejoice when they disgrace and shame him, knowing that the Holy One, blessed be He, loves him in sending him such light sufferings in order to purify his sins. And that one who disgraces him shall bear his own iniquity, for he is an evil strap used to strike this one, as it is said (Isaiah 10:5), "woe, Assyria, rod of My anger," and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:26: And it is fitting that he pray to the Holy One, blessed be He, in all his prayers - morning, afternoon, evening - that the Holy One, blessed be He, grant him the merit of the attribute of humility and submission, and that he be joyful in these sufferings if he is shamed and provoked, and in all the other attributes of humility written in this Gate, and pray for all of them - and through this he shall be reconciled to the Holy One, blessed be He, and atonement shall be granted him for what he has sinned until now in anger and pride. And since this is his request, he shall not become angry and shall not respond to whoever disgraces him. These two ways to acquiring humility I heard from the mouth of my teacher, peace be upon him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:27: And I further heard that it is impossible for a person to attain the merit of holiness and repentance until he acquires in his heart the attribute of humility properly and the attribute of anger departs from him entirely - for one of the twenty-four things that delay repentance is being a wrathful person. And further, that he shall toil greatly to attain the acquisition of holiness, and when he becomes angry for a single moment everything departs, and it is found that all his toil was for naught and all his days were spent in vanity - and when he returns in repentance he shall toil greatly until he is sanctified, and would that he be sanctified - and if he becomes angry again, he has lost all he did and toiled in vain, as explained, and there is no end to the matter, that he acquire holiness through it, until he acquires through it the attribute of humility in its completeness, with the conditions to be explained in it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:28: And Rabbeinu Tam wrote in Sefer HaYashar (Gate 6) that the wise, when they enter repentance, should swear a severe oath not to become angry, and he elaborated on this. And I say that the oath should be only not to become angry except over a matter that the Torah permitted to be angered by, such as against the wicked, as King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 139:21), "do I not hate those who hate You, LORD, and loathe those who rise against You" - and likewise to be angry with a student, as it is said (Ketubot 103b), "cast bile among the students" - and if he becomes angry over other matters, he shall fine himself with a known penalty that shall cause him distress, and not release himself from his oath, to fulfill what is said (Psalms 15:4), "he swears to his own harm and does not retract." And he should conduct himself this way for a year or two, until he acquires through it the attribute of humility.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:29: And I further say that it is good for a person to make a short reminder of the punishments of anger and pride, and the merits of humility, to read them every day - this device is also a fine one, for who is the fool who would wish to sustain great loss for a small gain? Rather, at the time of anger he forgets all the punishments and all the merits he shall lose - and when he persists in reading, the learning shall bring him to action, and he shall be diligent and careful.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:30: And I say further, that this second aspect can be confirmed from the teaching of our Rabbis, of blessed memory, in the Midrash (Shemot Rabbah, Parashat 34), on the verse (Exodus 25:10), "and they shall make an ark of acacia wood" - these are their words: Elihu came and said (Job 37:23), "Shaddai, we cannot find Him, exalted in power" - whoever hears this verse says, perhaps this is a blasphemy, God forbid - rather, Elihu meant this: we did not find the power of the Holy One, blessed be He's might, exercised with His creatures, for the Holy One, blessed be He, does not come with burdens against His creatures; He does not come upon a person except according to his own strength. You find that when the Holy One, blessed be He, gave the Torah to Israel, had He come upon them with the full force of His power, they would not have been able to withstand it, as it is said (Deuteronomy 5:22), "if we hear again," and so on - rather, He came upon them only according to their own strength, as it is said (Psalms 29:4), "the voice of the LORD is with power [bakoach]" - it does not say "with His power" [bekocho] but "with power" [bakoach] - the power of each and every one - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:31: And from this teaching is understood the rebuke I wrote in the name of my teacher, peace be upon him: for if they say to a person, why did you not perform mortifications and fastings, he may say that he did not have the strength for them, and the Holy One, blessed be He, does not come with burdens against His creatures - but if they say to him, why did you become angry and cast off from yourself the fear of Heaven, what shall he answer his Creator? Is his evil inclination not something that must be overcome, and is it not within a person's own power over it, without any mortification at all, but merely that he take it to heart and accept upon himself that he not be exacting and not insist on his own rights? For (Psalms 10:12/Deuteronomy 10:12), "what does the LORD your God ask of you" - for fear is with you, so much so that you need not seek after it through a loss of money and the like, matters that are external to you.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:32: And there is further confirmation for my teacher's rebukes in the verses of the Prophets and the Writings - the first, what the prophet wrote (Zephaniah 2:3), "seek righteousness, seek humility." And further what is said (Lamentations 3:30), "let him give his cheek to the one who strikes him; let him be filled with disgrace; let him put his mouth in the dust."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:33: And further he should think of what King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 15:4), "despised in his own eyes and rejected [nim'as]" - for it is known that if he is despised in his own eyes and thinks himself rejected, he shall not respond to his own disgrace. And "rejected" is that he think of the inferiority and lowliness of his own soul, that he is rejected in the eyes of the Creator because of his evil deeds; and further, that he think of his own repulsiveness in his life and in his death - whether, in life, from the worms and lice on his head, as they, of blessed memory, explained (see Kohelet Rabbah 5:12), "how much more so man, who is a worm" (Job 25:6) - these are the lice on the head; and in his death, "the son of man, a worm" (ibid.) - being repugnant from the aspect of decay and the foul odor within his own bowels, as they, of blessed memory, explained, that at the time a person enters the privy, they say to him, see your own end - and when he thinks of this, certainly he shall not respond to his own disgrace.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:34: And with this intent the Tanna said (Avot, chapter 4, mishnah 4): Rabbi Levitas, a man of Yavneh, says, be exceedingly, exceedingly lowly of spirit, for the hope of man is the worm. And many explanations have been said of this mishnah, and it appears to me that in saying "for the hope of man is the worm," since we hold that anything destined to be done is considered as already done - if so, since the hope of man is to become entirely worm, he should think that already, while still alive, he is partly worm - and the proof is the lice on the head, as they, of blessed memory, explained in the Midrash, "how much more so man, who is a worm" - these are the lice on the head. And once he thinks of this, he shall be lowly in his own soul's eyes, for if he considers himself, when insulted, as already dead and full of worms, he shall not pay attention to what is said, for he shall think in his heart and say, would a dead man, full of worms, respond to his own disgrace? Certainly he would not respond, for that would be outside of reason.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:35: Further, my teacher wrote a way to acquire humility, which is that he should always strive to flee from honor, and choose the lowliest of places, and likewise strive to honor all creatures, poor and rich alike, treating them as equal - for there is no difference between the rich and the poor except in money, but both were created in image and likeness - and whoever honors creatures honors the supernal Craftsman who made them in His likeness, and if, God forbid, he disgraces them, it is as though he disgraces the Craftsman who made them - along the lines of what they said in Tractate Ta'anit (20b) concerning Rabbi Elazar, who encountered a very ugly man, and so on, and said to him, go to the craftsman who made me and tell him, how ugly is this vessel You have made - until he had to ask his forgiveness, and he said to him, I forgive you, forgive me. Further, that he always think of his own disgrace, his lack of understanding, his repugnant decay, and that he is worm and maggot.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:36: Further, I heard from his mouth that when they disgrace and shame him, he should think that Samael stands accusing him above, and that this is a strap drawn from him - for it is written (Proverbs 16:7), "when the LORD is pleased with a man's ways, He makes even his enemies be at peace with him" - and therefore King David, peace be upon him, for the atonement of his sin, was silent when Shimi ben Gera disgraced him, calling him a man of blood (II Samuel 16:7), an adulterer, a bastard, wicked, an oppressor, an abomination - as Rashi, of blessed memory, explained on (I Kings 2:8), "and he cursed me with a severe [nimretzet] curse" - an acrostic, as explained [see above 17:42] - for he knew that Shimi was an agent from above to strike him with his tongue, and in his deeds, that he threw dust, and so on (II Samuel 16:13), and he said, for the LORD told him to curse David - and who shall say, why have you done so? - therefore he should worry about his own sins and not respond to his own disgrace.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:37: And along these lines the pious author wrote in Chovot HaLevavot, Gate 5 (Gate of Unity of Deed, chapter 5), that this is the matter of (Avot, chapter 3, mishnah 10), "whoever is pleasing to people is pleasing to the Omnipresent" - for whoever is good in His eyes, blessed be He, the Holy One, blessed be He, plants His love in the eyes of creatures, that they love him. It follows that if they disgrace him, it is fitting for him to be silent, for certainly the spirit of the Omnipresent is not pleased with him, and he should worry about his own sins.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:38: Further, he should think that everything his disgracer says of him is true, that he has not said even one part in a thousand of his sins - as the liturgical poet said, "if my neighbors reproved me for my sins, they would flee and distance themselves far from my borders" - and although they harm him, their harm does not reach what he himself has blemished above, for he has not taken as severely as he himself has done, being a slanderer separating an intimate friend [see Proverbs 16:28] - and how can he ignore the great war that Samael wages against him over his sins, and be preoccupied with the small war? This is what I have heard.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:39: And I say a great rebuke for acquiring humility, and for not responding to his own disgrace, and not becoming angry - it is a parable of a certain man who went to the king and entreated him, prostrating himself before him, that he come to dwell with him - and the king, out of his great humility, agreed to dwell with him in his house. As time passed, this man performed disgraceful acts before the king, until the king fled from him. Would it not certainly be a disgrace to such a man, and should we not say of him that he is far from the discipline of decent people? For by doing those things before the king, he is found to have driven the king from his house by force - for the king cannot bear that a chamber pot of filth be brought before him until he flees, or that they crown a servant in his place and expel the king - and it was he himself who had entreated the king to come dwell with him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:40: And the parable's meaning is understood: for we, the people of Israel - all our prayers, our mitzvot, and our Torah are to draw the Shechinah to dwell with us, as it is said (Exodus 25:8), "and let them make Me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them" - among them literally, within their own hearts. And this premise is explained in the Zohar, the Tikkunim, and in several places, that Israel "form the image" [tzarin tzurah] - and so in the Zohar (Parashat Terumah, page 133a), that whoever prepares a bed, a table, a chair, and a lamp for the Holy One, blessed be He, the Holy One, blessed be He, shall be his guest every day, and it explains there the matter in the secret of prayer; see there. And it is known that the King's dwelling is a broken and crushed heart, as we have explained, and its opposite is anger and pride.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:41: It follows that the angry person crowns the servant who denies the foundational principle, and expels the Shechinah that had dwelt in the soul within his heart - and therefore the soul departs, and likewise the Shechinah, as explained - and therefore the Shechinah, without doubt, shall not dwell with a person who casts her from her place and expels her whenever he wishes, but rather, once the Shechinah knows with certainty that he has already accepted upon himself not to become angry again, then she shall return to dwell with him - and this is what Rashbi, peace be upon him, said in the teaching from Parashat Tetzaveh (page 182a) that we copied above, "only if the person comes and uproots it entirely and forever, and afterward strives to sanctify himself and draw holiness upon himself" - meaning, drawing the holiness of his soul that departed from him, and likewise drawing the Shechinah, for the dwelling of the Shechinah is in the soul.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:42: And for the reason of this parable, together with Rashbi's teaching, peace be upon him (Zohar, Parashat Beshalach, page 55b), which we copied in the Gate of Love, chapter 6, concerning "your friend and your father's friend" - see there. And this parable is also a moral lesson for all the sins by which a person sins against the Shechinah, for certainly he thereby expels her from himself, since all transgressions are the stench of the husk, and a king cannot bear anything but a good scent from Torah and mitzvot. And this is what it said there, on the verse (Proverbs 25:17), "let your foot be rare in your neighbor's house" - "let your inclination be rare," so that it not boil against you and not rule over you, and so on, as explained there, that through every deed of the evil inclination, which he gives it dominion over him, he drives away the holy soul and the Shechinah from him - and this is not fitting, since He is "your friend and your father's friend," as explained there, that He wishes to dwell with you - that you should perform deeds that would drive Him from your house.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:43: Further, for another reason it is fitting that he not become angry: for he thereby nullifies the mitzvah to fear the glorious and awesome Name (Deuteronomy 28:58) - for whoever is before the king and fears him does not become angry before him, but is ashamed and afraid of him, and leaves all his affairs to the king, since it is in his power to repair everything, and perhaps that very disgracer is acting by the king's own authority, as King David, peace be upon him, said (II Samuel 16:10), "the LORD has told him to curse." And so Shmuel said in Nedarim (22b), in the teaching we copied above in the previous chapter, whoever becomes angry - even the Shechinah is not considered important compared to him - it is not necessary to mention his own soul, hewn from beneath the Throne of Glory, whom the angels honor, and his fellows, made in image and likeness, whom he must honor, since "who is honored? He who honors creatures" - but even the Shechinah, whose glory fills the whole earth, whom he must fear - and this is (Psalms 10:4), "God is not in all his schemes" - the explanation of "all" [kol] is that not one thought of his own thoughts is [directed] against the Name; and "kol" is like the matter of "you shall do no [kol] work" (Exodus 20:10), and there are many similar cases. And through this is explained what is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Naso, page 145a), that whoever has fear has humility and piety; see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:44: And when a person takes to heart that all the causes that befall him all come from Him, blessed be He, since He watches over every single detail - for they said (Chullin 7b), a person does not even bruise his finger below unless it is proclaimed against him from above - he shall not become angry at the deed of the LORD. And of something similar to this King Solomon, peace be upon him, said (Proverbs 16:3), "commit your deeds to the LORD, and your plans shall be established."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:45: Further, for another reason it is fitting that he not respond to whoever disgraces him: the warning of King Solomon, peace be upon him (Proverbs 26:4), "do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you too become like him." And one must be precise about the doubling in his words, saying "fool" and "his folly." And further, the words "you too" are superfluous, since he already said "lest you become like him." And one can say that Scripture gave three reasons not to answer a fool. The first is precise in saying "according to his folly" - meaning that since he is a fool, the husk, which is his folly, has clothed itself in him to say those things, and he is like a barking dog, whom it is not fitting to be concerned about. And a second argument: "lest you become like him" - for since his words have had an effect within his own heart, causing him to cease from holiness and words of Torah, the husk has also entered his own heart, since out of anger he answered him - it follows that he becomes exactly equal to the fool, for the fool who became angry and answered in folly - certainly they did something to him worthy of being upset about, and his answer is called his own folly; likewise the wise man who answers him, because his words made an impression upon him, behold he is like him - for it is fitting that a wise man in the wisdom of Torah not let vain words make an impression on his heart, even if there be disgrace to him - and the proof of this is Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, when Aaron and Miriam spoke against him, it is written there (Numbers 12:3), "and the man Moses was very humble" - and the commentators explained that he heard and was silent and did not take it to heart to respond, and the reason is that from the abundance of his cleaving to the Name, he did not concern himself with responding to worldly matters, and the Name answered on his behalf. And a third [reason]: "you too" - meaning, the soul that is with you - and this is hinted at in the word "atah" [you], for the essential part of a person called "you" is the soul, since the body ceases and is lost and has no permanence to be called "you," and when a person speaks with his fellow, he does not speak with his body but with his soul, which sees and hears. And in the plural [implication] it hints that the Shechinah too departs, as explained in the teaching we copied from Parashat Tetzaveh, that from the angry person, his soul and the Shechinah depart.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:46: And the pious Rabbi Yosef Yavetz wrote, on the mishnah (Avot, chapter 4, mishnah 4), "be exceedingly, exceedingly lowly of spirit," fitting words for this discourse - I saw fit to copy them here. He raised a difficulty, that the Tanna should have said "your hope is a worm," since he began in the second person by saying "be." And he, of blessed memory, resolved this by saying that pride is of two kinds, and corresponding to them two kinds of lowliness. One: the proud person who thinks that honor is fitting for him and that all should honor him, while he does not honor anyone, like a king and princes. And the correct attribute in this is that he honor every person according to his own level, and think that he and they were created for His honor, blessed be He, and it is not fitting to make use of His creatures, made in image and likeness - and this is the attribute mentioned above. And concerning this kind of pride our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (see Sotah 5a), the Holy One, blessed be He, said of pride, I and it cannot dwell in one place - and the reason is as I have written, that honor is fitting for Him, blessed be He, since there is none above Him, and this is what He said (Psalms 93:1), "the LORD reigns, He is clothed in pride."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:47: And the second is one who disgraces people, insults and abuses them, since they are considered by him as nothing and void - and concerning this He warned, "do not despise any person." And the correct attribute is to be silent, not to respond to his own disgrace, and for this he must be very lowly in his own eyes, like mere dust, so as not to feel it at all. And for this the Tanna said, "be exceedingly, exceedingly lowly of spirit" - if others disgrace you, do not be dismayed by them and their abuse - and he gave the reason, "for the hope of man" - for that arrogant man who disgraced and abused you, tomorrow the worm shall consume him, and what is his disgrace to you? And this is the reason it says "enosh" [man] and not "adam," which would have been more fitting, since man [adam] is taken from dust - but rather it intended what was said, to warn the one who is insulted.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:48: And consider, reader, this explanation, for it agrees from every side - and Isaiah, peace be upon him, aroused me to this explanation by saying (Isaiah 51:7), "listen to me, you who know righteousness, the people in whose heart is My law; fear not the disgrace of man [enosh], nor be dismayed at their revilings, for the moth shall eat them like a garment, and the worm shall eat them like wool, but My salvation shall be forever, and My righteousness for generations of generations." Behold, the Tanna mentioned the language that the prophet said, "for the hope of man is the worm" - but he first said, "listen to me, you who know righteousness, the people in whose heart is My law," for people of this level are few, since from the first kind you shall find many people who honor others, each according to his own level - but that one hear his own disgrace and be silent - there is not even one; and whoever does so shows the greatness of his own attachment to the supernal world, "with gods whose dwelling is not with flesh" (Daniel 2:11) - and therefore he shall not feel the disgrace of the world - and for this King Solomon, peace be upon him, said (Proverbs 14:29), "he who is slow to anger has great understanding," "every man," and so on (ibid. 19:11) - and in the mishnah "who is honored" I have explained this with the help of Heaven.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:49: And so that my words enter your ears, I shall give you a parable of a man who had two pearls: one, beyond all value, worth a thousand thousand thousand gold dinars, and the other worth a thousand gold pieces - and the second was stolen from him. Is it conceivable that this man should grieve, when the other, first pearl remains, which lacks nothing? So too people whose souls are very holy, and who have come to perceive their [true] world in their lifetime, shall not concern themselves with the loss of the goods of this world, and all of it is like the peel of garlic in their eyes - they shall not rejoice at its increase nor grieve at its loss.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:50: My masters and my geniuses, look and see: the supernal holy one, Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa, for whose sake the whole world was sustained, and who was content with a kav of carobs from Sabbath eve to Sabbath eve (Berachot 17b); and Elijah, peace be upon him, "girded with a girdle of leather about his loins" (II Kings 1:8), and his meal was a cake baked on coals and a jug of water (I Kings 19:6) - this is nothing but the strength of their faith in their Creator and the intensity of their attachment and cleaving to Him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:51: And for this the prophet said, "who know righteousness, the people in whose heart is My law" - for this attribute is found only in one whose 248 organs and 365 sinews desire Torah, which grows in his heart this supernal attribute of which they said (Avodah Zarah 20b), humility is greater than all of them, and it is what brings one to the Holy Spirit, as it says (Isaiah 61:1), "the spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me to bring good tidings to the humble; He has sent me to bind up the brokenhearted" - and these are the ones who ascend to this great and wondrous level. And this is the conclusion of the words of the prophet, peace be upon him, "but My salvation shall be forever, and My righteousness for generations of generations" - for God, blessed be He, is destined to raise the horn of the insulted, who hear their own disgrace and do not respond.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:52: And know that the clear proof upon a person, whether the Name is continually before him, is the fruit of the whole Torah, in saying (Deuteronomy 10:20), "the LORD your God you shall fear, Him you shall serve, and to Him you shall cleave" - lowliness, and its opposite is pride. And I shall give you a parable of this: two men each have a thousand dinars - one in a village where all its people do not attain a thousand gold dinars - there is no doubt that this one shall be proud among the villagers; the second dwells in Tyre, whose merchants are princes - this one shall consider his own wealth lowly in his eyes and count it as nothing. So too, whoever is far from the Name, blessed be He, and from His angels and His pious ones, is proud over those below him; but the righteous, before whom the Name is continually present, shall be lowly before Him, down to the dust - for by looking at the greatness of the Name and His angels and His pious ones from the beginning of time, they shall become very lowly in their own eyes - and one of the eleven principles of the Torah is, "despised in his own eyes and rejected" (Psalms 15:4).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:53: And see the testimony of Solomon, peace be upon him (Proverbs 15:28), concerning everything we have said: "the heart of the righteous meditates on how to answer, but the mouth of the wicked pours forth evil things; the LORD is far from the wicked, but He hears the prayer of the righteous." It means: the heart of the righteous constantly meditates on what shall lead him to humility and lowliness; but the wicked are not content with their hearts being proud, but even bring forth their pride with their mouths, so that they constantly "pour forth evil things." And the reason for this is that "the LORD is far from the wicked," and they do not meditate on Him; but the righteous - "He hears their prayer," since they are continually holy to Him.
